# Question 20 ★ - Deducing a password

## Original question

I have forgotten my 5-character computer password, but I know that it consists of the letters
$a,b,c,d,e$ in some order. When I enter a potential password into the computer, it tells me exactly **how
many** of the letters are in the correct position.

When I enter **abcde**, it tells me that **none** of the letters are in the correct position. The same happens
when I enter **cdbea** and **eadbc**.

Using the best strategy, how many **further** attempts must I make in order to **guarantee** that I can
**deduce** the correct password?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** None: I can deduce it immediately &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** One &nbsp;&nbsp; **C** Two
&nbsp;&nbsp; **D** Three &nbsp;&nbsp; **E** More than three

---

## Concepts first - what the machine is actually telling you

::: {.callout-tip}
## The feedback is a number, not a yes or no

This is the whole question. The computer does not say "right" or "wrong" — it returns **how many letters sit
in the correct position**, a number from $0$ to $5$. One guess therefore does not split the possibilities into
two; it splits them into as many groups as there are possible answers.

So a single guess can, at best, tell apart as many passwords as there are distinct feedback values. Counting
those values is the first thing to do, not the last.

**A free restriction.** The password and every guess are **rearrangements of the same five letters**. If four
of the five letters are in the correct position, the fifth has nowhere else to go — so it is correct too.
Feedback $4$ is **impossible**, and the possible values are

$$0,\ 1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 5 \qquad\text{— five of them.}$$
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## What "guarantee" means

"How many attempts must I make to **guarantee** that I can deduce the password" is a **worst-case** question,
not a lucky-guess question. An answer of *One* means: there is a single guess such that **whatever number it
comes back with**, only one candidate is left standing.

So you are not asked to find the password. You are asked to find a guess whose five possible replies separate
the survivors.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Method - turning "none are correct" into a grid

1. **Translate each guess into eliminations.** "abcde gives $0$" means
   $a$ is not in position 1, $b$ not in position 2, $c$ not in position 3, $d$ not in position 4, $e$ not in
   position 5. One guess with feedback $0$ removes exactly one letter from each position.
2. **Build the position grid.** Five positions, five letters, and strike out what each guess forbids.
3. **Read off the survivors**, remembering the answer must still be a permutation — no letter twice.
4. **Count them.** If one survivor is left, the answer is *None*. Otherwise compare the count with the number
   of available feedback values and look for a single separating guess.
5. **Check that a separating guess exists** — the count being small enough makes it possible, not certain.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**Step 1 — the eliminations.** Each of the three guesses returned $0$, so each one forbids one letter in each
position:

| position | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| abcde forbids | $a$ | $b$ | $c$ | $d$ | $e$ |
| cdbea forbids | $c$ | $d$ | $b$ | $e$ | $a$ |
| eadbc forbids | $e$ | $a$ | $d$ | $b$ | $c$ |
| **left over** | $b,d$ | $c,e$ | $a,e$ | $a,c$ | $b,d$ |

*The three guesses were chosen so that no letter is forbidden twice in the same position — so every position
loses three different letters and keeps exactly two.*

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-cap: "The elimination grid. Three guesses knock out three letters in every position, leaving two candidates per position."
rows = list("abcde")
forb = {"abcde": BLUE, "cdbea": RED, "eadbc": GREEN}
grid = {}
for g, col in forb.items():
    for i, ch in enumerate(g):
        grid[(ch, i)] = col
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 3.6))
for i in range(5):
    for j, ch in enumerate(rows):
        y = 4 - j
        if (ch, i) in grid:
            ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((i, y), 1, 1, color=grid[(ch, i)], alpha=0.22))
            ax.plot([i+0.18, i+0.82], [y+0.18, y+0.82], color=grid[(ch, i)], lw=1.6)
            ax.plot([i+0.18, i+0.82], [y+0.82, y+0.18], color=grid[(ch, i)], lw=1.6)
        else:
            ax.text(i+0.5, y+0.5, ch, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=13, fontweight="bold")
for i in range(6):
    ax.plot([i, i], [0, 5], color="0.75", lw=0.8)
    ax.plot([0, 5], [i, i], color="0.75", lw=0.8)
ax.set_xticks(np.arange(5)+0.5); ax.set_xticklabels([f"pos {i+1}" for i in range(5)], fontsize=9)
ax.set_yticks(np.arange(5)+0.5); ax.set_yticklabels(rows[::-1], fontsize=11)
ax.set_xlim(0, 5); ax.set_ylim(0, 5)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
for sp in ax.spines.values(): sp.set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(length=0)
handles = [plt.Line2D([], [], color=c, lw=2, label=g) for g, c in forb.items()]
ax.legend(handles=handles, fontsize=8, loc="upper center",
          bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.09), ncol=3, frameon=False,
          title="struck out by", title_fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**Step 2 — the survivors.** The grid allows

$$\text{pos 1}\in\{b,d\},\quad \text{pos 2}\in\{c,e\},\quad \text{pos 3}\in\{a,e\},\quad
\text{pos 4}\in\{a,c\},\quad \text{pos 5}\in\{b,d\}$$

which is $2^{5}=32$ strings, but most repeat a letter. *Positions 1 and 5 both draw from $\{b,d\}$, so they
must take one each; the same for positions 2 and 4 drawing $c$, and for 3 and 4 drawing $a$.* Keeping only the
genuine permutations leaves exactly **four**:

$$\textbf{bcead},\qquad \textbf{beacd},\qquad \textbf{dceab},\qquad \textbf{deacb}.$$

So **A is wrong** — four candidates is not a deduction.

**Step 3 — can one more attempt always finish it?** There are four candidates and five possible feedback
values, so it is not ruled out. And a guess that works is easy to find: **guess one of the four candidates**,
say **bcead**. Counting matches against each candidate:

| if the password is | bcead | beacd | dceab | deacb |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| feedback from guessing **bcead** | $5$ | $2$ | $3$ | $0$ |

*All four replies are different, so whatever number comes back identifies the password uniquely — and if the
reply is $5$ the guess was simply right.*

One further attempt is enough, and four candidates means none is not. **B**

**Where the mark went.** Choosing **C** (*Two*) is what you get by imagining the attempts as yes/no tests:
with four candidates, testing them one at a time, you would expect to need two or three. *But the machine
answers with a number, not a yes or no — a single guess sorts the four candidates into four different
buckets.* Reading the feedback as one bit of information instead of roughly $\log_2 5$ bits is the whole
error.

:::

## Question 20 practice

::: {.question}
1. Suppose only the first two guesses had been made — **abcde** and **cdbea**, both returning $0$.
   &nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** How many candidates remain?
   &nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Can one further attempt guarantee the password? How many are needed?
2. Explain carefully why a single further attempt can never distinguish more than **five** candidates.
3. Prove that the feedback can never be exactly $4$.
4. A **four**-character version: the password uses $a,b,c,d$ in some order, and both **abcd** and **cdab**
   return $0$.
   &nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** List the candidates.
   &nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** There are four of them, as in the exam question. Is one further attempt enough this
   time? Explain what is different.
5. Back in the exam question, is guessing one of the four candidates the **only** kind of guess that works, or
   do non-candidates work too? What is the advantage of guessing a candidate?
6. Harder. Suppose the three guesses returning $0$ had been **abcde**, **badec** and **cedab** instead. How
   many candidates remain, and how many further attempts are then needed?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

1. **(a) 13.** *Two guesses forbid only two letters per position, leaving three per position, and far more of
   those combinations survive as permutations.*
   **(b) No — two are needed.** *With $13$ candidates and only five possible replies, the best any single
   guess can do is split them $4\,/\,4\,/\,4\,/\,1$, so some reply still leaves four candidates standing.*
   Two further attempts are enough.
2. The feedback is one of $0,1,2,3,5$ — five values. *A guess sorts the candidates into groups by the reply
   they would produce, and candidates in the same group are indistinguishable. With six or more candidates,
   two must share a reply by the pigeonhole principle.*
3. If four positions hold the correct letter, the remaining position holds the only letter not yet used — *and
   that letter is forced to be the correct one, because the password uses each letter exactly once.* So four
   matches always means five.
4. **(a)** badc, bcda, dabc, dcba.
   **(b) No.** *For four-letter permutations the possible feedbacks are $0,1,2,4$ — only four values — and no
   single guess happens to spread these four candidates across four different replies.* Having few enough
   candidates makes a one-guess finish **possible**, not automatic: you still have to produce the guess. This
   is exactly why step 5 of the method is there.
5. Non-candidates work too — there are $28$ guesses in all that separate the four. *The advantage of guessing
   a candidate is that it might simply be right, so you can finish in that attempt rather than merely learn
   the answer and have to type it afterwards.*
6. **3 candidates**, and one further attempt is still enough. *Fewer candidates survive because those three
   guesses overlap — some position is forbidden the same letter twice — so the eliminations are less
   efficient than the exam's three.*

:::

# Question 12 - Ordering $\sin 2x$, $\cos 2x$ and $\tan x$

## Original question

The diagram shows the graphs of $y=\sin 2x$ and $y=\cos 2x$ for $-\tfrac\pi2<x<\tfrac\pi2$.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-cap: "The two curves given in the question. tan x is not drawn — adding it is the first thing to do."
xs = np.linspace(-np.pi/2 + 1e-3, np.pi/2 - 1e-3, 1200)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.4))
ax.plot(xs, np.sin(2*xs), color=BLUE, lw=2, label=r"$y=\sin 2x$")
ax.plot(xs, np.cos(2*xs), color=RED, lw=2, label=r"$y=\cos 2x$")
ax.axhline(0, color=GREY, lw=0.8); ax.axvline(0, color=GREY, lw=0.8)
for v in (-np.pi/2, np.pi/2):
    ax.axvline(v, color="0.6", lw=1.0, ls=":")
ax.set_xticks([-np.pi/2, -np.pi/4, 0, np.pi/4, np.pi/2])
ax.set_xticklabels([r"$-\frac{\pi}{2}$", r"$-\frac{\pi}{4}$", "0", r"$\frac{\pi}{4}$", r"$\frac{\pi}{2}$"])
ax.set_ylim(-1.6, 1.6)
ax.set_xlabel("x"); ax.set_ylabel("y")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower left")
ax.grid(alpha=0.18)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Which one of the following is **not** true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $\cos 2x<\sin 2x<\tan x$ for some real number $x$ with $-\tfrac\pi2<x<\tfrac\pi2$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $\cos 2x<\tan x<\sin 2x$ for some real number $x$ with $-\tfrac\pi2<x<\tfrac\pi2$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $\sin 2x<\cos 2x<\tan x$ for some real number $x$ with $-\tfrac\pi2<x<\tfrac\pi2$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $\sin 2x<\tan x<\cos 2x$ for some real number $x$ with $-\tfrac\pi2<x<\tfrac\pi2$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $\tan x<\sin 2x<\cos 2x$ for some real number $x$ with $-\tfrac\pi2<x<\tfrac\pi2$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** $\tan x<\cos 2x<\sin 2x$ for some real number $x$ with $-\tfrac\pi2<x<\tfrac\pi2$

---

## The method to recall

::: {.callout-tip}
## Five of the six are true, so hunt for the one that is impossible

Each option says "**for some** $x$", so an option is true as soon as you can point at a single $x$ that
works. Five of the six will fall out of a decent sketch in seconds. The marks are all in the sixth — the one
you have to **prove impossible**, and for that a sketch is not enough.

So: sketch first to clear away the easy five, then argue about the survivor.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Memorise this box

**Add the missing curve.** The diagram gives you two of the three expressions. Draw $y=\tan x$ on the same
axes before anything else: it passes through the origin, increases throughout
$-\tfrac\pi2<x<\tfrac\pi2$, and shoots off to $\pm\infty$ at the two ends.

**To show an ordering is impossible, cut the problem in two:**

1. Find the exact set of $x$ on which the **first** inequality holds. Use the harmonic form:
   $$\cos 2x-\sin 2x=\sqrt2\,\cos\!\left(2x+\tfrac\pi4\right),$$
   so $\sin 2x<\cos 2x$ exactly when $-\tfrac\pi2<2x+\tfrac\pi4<\tfrac\pi2$, i.e. on
   $-\tfrac{3\pi}8<x<\tfrac\pi8$.
2. On **that interval only**, show the second inequality always fails. Bounding each side separately on a few
   sub-intervals is usually enough — you rarely need calculus.

**Useful exact values:** $\tan\tfrac\pi8=\sqrt2-1\approx0.414$ and $\cos\tfrac\pi4=\tfrac{\sqrt2}2\approx0.707$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-cap: "All three curves. The shaded strip is where sin 2x < cos 2x; throughout it the tan curve (green) stays below the cos curve, which is why one ordering is unreachable."
xs = np.linspace(-np.pi/2 + 1e-3, np.pi/2 - 1e-3, 3000)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.0, 4.0))
ax.plot(xs, np.sin(2*xs), color=BLUE, lw=2, label=r"$y=\sin 2x$")
ax.plot(xs, np.cos(2*xs), color=RED, lw=2, label=r"$y=\cos 2x$")
ax.plot(xs, np.tan(xs), color=GREEN, lw=2, label=r"$y=\tan x$")
ax.axvspan(-3*np.pi/8, np.pi/8, color=AMBER, alpha=0.13)
ax.text(-0.62, 1.72, r"$\sin 2x<\cos 2x$ here", color=AMBER, fontsize=9)
ax.axhline(0, color=GREY, lw=0.8); ax.axvline(0, color=GREY, lw=0.8)
ax.set_xticks([-np.pi/2, -3*np.pi/8, -np.pi/4, 0, np.pi/8, np.pi/2])
ax.set_xticklabels([r"$-\frac{\pi}{2}$", r"$-\frac{3\pi}{8}$", r"$-\frac{\pi}{4}$", "0",
                    r"$\frac{\pi}{8}$", r"$\frac{\pi}{2}$"], fontsize=9)
ax.set_ylim(-2.2, 2.2)
ax.set_xlabel("x"); ax.set_ylabel("y")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right")
ax.grid(alpha=0.18)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**The five that are true.** Reading the picture:

| | ordering | a witness |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | $\cos 2x<\sin 2x<\tan x$ | $x=\tfrac{3\pi}8$: $\cos\tfrac{3\pi}4<\sin\tfrac{3\pi}4<\tan\tfrac{3\pi}8$ |
| **B** | $\cos 2x<\tan x<\sin 2x$ | $x\approx0.64$ |
| **D** | $\sin 2x<\tan x<\cos 2x$ | $x=-\tfrac\pi8$ |
| **E** | $\tan x<\sin 2x<\cos 2x$ | $x=0^{-}$, just left of the origin |
| **F** | $\tan x<\cos 2x<\sin 2x$ | $x\approx-1.32$ |

**Why C is impossible.** It asks for $\sin 2x<\cos 2x$ **and** $\cos 2x<\tan x$ at the same $x$.

*Step 1 — where does the first inequality hold?*

$$\cos 2x-\sin 2x=\sqrt2\,\cos\!\left(2x+\tfrac\pi4\right)>0
\iff -\tfrac\pi2<2x+\tfrac\pi4<\tfrac\pi2
\iff -\tfrac{3\pi}8<x<\tfrac\pi8 .$$

*Step 2 — on that interval, $\cos 2x$ is always above $\tan x$.* Split it into three pieces and bound each
side separately:

| interval | $\cos 2x$ | $\tan x$ | conclusion |
|---|---|---|---|
| $-\tfrac{3\pi}8<x<-\tfrac\pi4$ | $>\cos\tfrac{3\pi}4=-\tfrac{\sqrt2}2\approx-0.707$ | $<\tan\!\left(-\tfrac\pi4\right)=-1$ | $\cos 2x>-0.707>-1>\tan x$ |
| $-\tfrac\pi4\le x\le0$ | $\ge0$ | $\le0$ | $\cos 2x\ge0\ge\tan x$, equal nowhere |
| $0<x<\tfrac\pi8$ | $>\cos\tfrac\pi4=\tfrac{\sqrt2}2\approx0.707$ | $<\tan\tfrac\pi8=\sqrt2-1\approx0.414$ | $\cos 2x>0.707>0.414>\tan x$ |

*Both functions are monotone on each piece, so the endpoint values really are bounds for the whole piece.* So
$\cos 2x>\tan x$ everywhere that $\sin 2x<\cos 2x$, and the two halves of C can never hold together.

**C**

**Where the mark went.** Choosing **E** means rejecting an ordering that the picture already shows: just to
the left of the origin, $\tan x<0$, $\sin 2x<0$ but larger, and $\cos 2x\approx1$. *The five true options only
need one witness each — do not try to prove them in general, just find a point.* Spend the time on the one
that resists.

:::

## Question 12 practice

::: {.question}
1. Find the exact set of $x$ in $-\tfrac\pi2<x<\tfrac\pi2$ for which $\sin 2x>\cos 2x$.
2. Is there an $x$ in $-\tfrac\pi2<x<\tfrac\pi2$ with $\tan x<\cos 2x<\sin 2x$? Give a witness or prove not.
3. Solve $\cos 2x=\tan x$ has how many solutions in $-\tfrac\pi2<x<\tfrac\pi2$? Justify from the graphs.
4. Write $3\sin\theta+4\cos\theta$ in the form $R\cos(\theta-\alpha)$, and hence find the exact set of
   $\theta$ in $0<\theta<2\pi$ with $3\sin\theta+4\cos\theta>0$.
5. Harder. For which $x$ in $0<x<\tfrac\pi2$ is $\tan x>2\sin x$? Give the answer exactly.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

1. $\sin 2x-\cos 2x=\sqrt2\sin\!\left(2x-\tfrac\pi4\right)>0$, so $0<2x-\tfrac\pi4<\pi$, giving
   $\tfrac\pi8<x<\tfrac{5\pi}8$. Intersecting with $-\tfrac\pi2<x<\tfrac\pi2$ leaves
   $\boxed{\tfrac\pi8<x<\tfrac\pi2}$.
2. **Yes** — this is option F. *By question 1 the right-hand inequality holds on $\tfrac\pi8<x<\tfrac\pi2$ and
   also, by periodicity of the harmonic form, on $-\tfrac\pi2<x<-\tfrac{3\pi}8$; on that left piece
   $\tan x<\tan\!\left(-\tfrac{3\pi}8\right)\approx-2.41$ while $\cos 2x>-0.71$.* For example $x=-1.32$.
3. **One.** *$\tan x$ increases from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$ across the interval while $\cos 2x$ is bounded
   between $-1$ and $1$, so $\tan x-\cos 2x$ is negative at the left end, positive at the right end, and —
   since $\tan$ rises much faster than $\cos 2x$ can fall — crosses once.*
4. $R=\sqrt{3^{2}+4^{2}}=5$ and $\tan\alpha=\tfrac34$, so $3\sin\theta+4\cos\theta=5\cos(\theta-\alpha)$ with
   $\alpha=\arctan\tfrac34$. This is positive when $-\tfrac\pi2<\theta-\alpha<\tfrac\pi2$, i.e.
   $\boxed{0<\theta<\alpha+\tfrac\pi2}$ together with $\alpha+\tfrac{3\pi}2<\theta<2\pi$.
5. $\tan x>2\sin x \iff \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}>2\sin x$. *On $0<x<\tfrac\pi2$ both $\sin x>0$ and
   $\cos x>0$, so we may divide by $\sin x$ and multiply by $\cos x$ without reversing anything:*
   $1>2\cos x$, i.e. $\cos x<\tfrac12$, giving $\boxed{\tfrac\pi3<x<\tfrac\pi2}$.

:::

# The four that took too long

All four of these were answered **correctly**, but slowly. The point here is the cue that gets you there
quickly, not the full working.

## Question 7 — two exponential graphs &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.78em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">6:19</span>

::: {.question}
$y=a^{x}$ (solid, $a$ a positive real number) and $y=f(x)$ (dashed) are sketched on the same axes. The dashed
curve passes through the same point on the $y$-axis and rises **more steeply**. Which of these could be true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**1** $f(x)=b^{x}$ for some $b>a$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **2** $f(x)=b^{x}$ for some $b<a$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**3** $f(x)=a^{kx}$ for some $k>1$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **4** $f(x)=a^{kx}$ for some $k<1$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

The cue: **$a^{kx}=(a^{k})^{x}$**. Statements 1 and 3 are therefore the *same* statement in two costumes,
since $a>1$ and $k>1$ give $a^{k}>a$. *Once you see that, you only have to decide whether a steeper curve
means a bigger base — it does — and both 1 and 3 are in, both 2 and 4 are out.*

**E** (1 and 3 only)

**The time saving.** Rewrite every $a^{kx}$ as $(a^{k})^{x}$ the moment you see it; then all four statements
are about one thing, the size of the base.

:::

## Question 10 — a sufficient condition for a zero integral &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.78em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">7:51</span>

::: {.question}
$f(x)$ is a function defined for all real values of $x$. Which one of the following is a **sufficient**
condition for $\displaystyle\int_1^3 f(x)\,\mathrm dx=0$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $f(2)=0$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** $f(1)=f(3)=0$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **C** $f(-x)=-f(x)$ for all $x$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $f(x+2)=-f(2-x)$ for all $x$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **E** $f(x-2)=-f(2-x)$ for all $x$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

The cue: **the integral runs from $1$ to $3$, so the symmetry has to be about the midpoint $x=2$** — not
about the origin.

- **C** and **E** both say $f$ is odd **about $0$**. *Substituting $y=x-2$ turns E into $f(y)=-f(-y)$, which
  is exactly C — so they are the same condition, and two identical options can neither of them be the answer.*
  Neither controls what happens between $1$ and $3$: take $f(x)=x$, which is odd, yet
  $\int_1^3 x\,\mathrm dx=4$.
- **D** says $f(x+2)=-f(2-x)$. Putting $u=x+2$ gives $f(u)=-f(4-u)$: the graph has **rotational symmetry
  about the point $(2,0)$**, the midpoint of the interval. *Reflecting the integral through that point sends
  it to minus itself, so it must be zero.* Formally, substituting $t=4-x$,
  $$\int_1^3 f(x)\,\mathrm dx=\int_1^3 f(4-t)\,\mathrm dt=-\int_1^3 f(t)\,\mathrm dt,$$
  so the integral equals its own negative and is $0$.
- **A** and **B** fix $f$ at one or two points, which cannot control an area: $(x-2)^{2}$ and $(x-1)(x-3)$ are
  counterexamples.

**D**

**The time saving.** Two options that say the same thing can both be eliminated at once. *And "sufficient"
means you must argue forwards from the condition — testing a function that happens to have zero integral
checks necessity instead, which is the wrong direction.*

:::

## Question 11 — area after a vertical shift &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.78em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2:51</span>

::: {.question}
$f(x)$ is increasing with $f(0)=0$. The positive constants $a,b$ satisfy $a<b$. The area enclosed by
$y=f(x)$, the $x$-axis and the lines $x=a$, $x=b$ is $R$. Let $g(x)=f(x)+2f(b)$. What is the area enclosed by
$y=g(x)$, the $x$-axis and the lines $x=a$ and $x=b$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $R+(b-a)f(b)$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** $R+2(b-a)f(b)$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **C** $R+2f(b)-f(a)$
&nbsp;&nbsp; **D** $R+2f(b)$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **E** $R+(f(b))^{2}$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**F** $R+(f(b))^{2}-(f(a))^{2}$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **G** $R+2(f(b)-f(a))f(b)$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

The cue: **$2f(b)$ is a constant**, so $g$ is $f$ shifted **up** by a fixed amount, and the extra area is a
rectangle.

$$\int_a^b g(x)\,\mathrm dx=\int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm dx+\int_a^b 2f(b)\,\mathrm dx=R+2f(b)(b-a).$$

*The width of the rectangle is $b-a$ and its height is $2f(b)$ — the options that leave out the width (D) or
use a height difference (C, G) are the traps.* Since $f$ is increasing with $f(0)=0$ and $0<a<b$, we have
$f>0$ on $[a,b]$, so the region really is above the axis and nothing has to be split into signed pieces.

**B**

**The time saving.** Shift up by a constant $\Rightarrow$ add **constant $\times$ width**. There is nothing
to integrate.

:::

## Question 13 — standard form &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.78em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">5:11</span>

::: {.question}
The positive real numbers $a\times10^{-3}$, $b\times10^{-2}$ and $c\times10^{-1}$ are each in standard form,
and

$$\bigl(a\times10^{-3}\bigr)+\bigl(b\times10^{-2}\bigr)=\bigl(c\times10^{-1}\bigr).$$

Which of the following must be true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** $a>9$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **II** $b>9$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **III** $a<c$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **IV** $b<c$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

The cue: **"in standard form" is the hypothesis**, and it says $1\le a,b,c<10$. Write that down first; the
rest is arithmetic.

Multiplying the equation by $10^{3}$:

$$a+10b=100c .$$

Since $c\ge1$, the right-hand side is at least $100$. But $a<10$, so

$$10b>100-10=90\quad\Longrightarrow\quad b>9 .$$

So **II must be true**. The others need only one counterexample each:

| | claim | counterexample |
|---|---|---|
| **I** | $a>9$ | $a=1$, $b=9.9$, $c=1$ — check $1+99=100$ ✓ |
| **III** | $a<c$ | $a=5$, $b=9.5$, $c=1$ — check $5+95=100$ ✓, and $5>1$ |
| **IV** | $b<c$ | always false, since $b>9$ while $c<10$ needs $100c=a+10b<110$, so $c<1.1$ |

**B** (II only)

**The time saving.** *Convert the whole equation to integers in one step by multiplying by $10^{3}$, then use
the bounds $1\le a,b,c<10$ immediately.* The question is not about standard form at all once that is done.

:::
